title: Geometric fixed vectors are scalar extensions of scheme invariants
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $K$ be an algebraic closure of $k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $G$ be a smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] affine group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$. Let $d\geq0$ and let $W$ be a $d$-dimensional $k$-vector space with a rational $G$-action: for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$ there is an action of $G(R)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\operatorname{Spec}R,G)$ by $R$-linear automorphisms of $W_R=R\otimes_k W$, natural in $R$. Define
$$W^G=\{w\in W:g(1\otimes w)=1\otimes w\text{ in }W_R\text{ for every commutative }k\text{-algebra }R\text{ and }g\in G(R)\}.$$
The scalar-extended inclusion $K\otimes_k W^G\longrightarrow K\otimes_k W$ is injective and identifies its source with
$$\{z\in K\otimes_k W:g z=z\text{ for every }g\in G(K)\}.$$
In particular, a nonzero vector fixed by all geometric points exists if and only if $W^G\ne0$. No perfectness or connectedness assumption on $k$ or $G$ is made.

source.place: Propositions 4.31--4.33, printed p.96, and Corollary 4.34, printed p.97; geometric-point detection for a smooth group uses Propositions 1.10 and 1.17, printed pp.9--11, and 1.26(b), printed p.13. This is the invariant comparison used in Corollaries 14.9 and 14.12, printed pp.282--283.

proof.text: Write $G=\operatorname{Spec}A$, with its given $k$-algebra structure. The affine-pair characterization [lem-weil-pbc-lft-affine-pairs], applied to the whole source and $\operatorname{Spec}k$, says that $A$ is a finitely generated $k$-algebra. By [def-weil-affine-spectrum], points of $G(R)$ are exactly $k$-algebra maps $A\to R$. Let $u\in G(A)$ correspond to $1_A$. Naturality of the given action therefore says, for $g:A\to R$ and $w\in W$, that $g(1\otimes w)$ is obtained from $u(1\otimes w)\in A\otimes_k W$ by applying $g\otimes1$.

source.place: Proposition 4.33, p.96, universal element; finite generation: Stacks Tag 01T2, lemma-locally-finite-type-characterize

proof.text: Define the $k$-linear map $D:W\to A\otimes_k W$ by $D(w)=u(1\otimes w)-1\otimes w$. Then $\ker D=W^G$: one inclusion follows by taking $R=A$, $g=u$ in the definition of $W^G$; the other follows by applying every $g\otimes1$ to $D(w)=0$ and using step 1. For any commutative $k$-algebra $B$, put $D_B=1_B\otimes D$ and identify its target with $(B\otimes_k A)\otimes_k W$ by rearranging pure tensors. If $z=\sum_i b_i\otimes w_i\in B\otimes_k W$ and $g:A\to B$ is a point, the map $b\otimes a\mapsto b\,g(a)$ sends $D_B(z)$ to $gz-z$. This follows term by term from step 1 and the $B$-linearity of the action. The multiplication map used here is the algebra tensor-product universal map of [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property].

source.place: Proposition 4.33, p.96; expand the universal-element calculation on pure tensors

proof.text: The image of $K\otimes_k W^G\to K\otimes_k W$ is exactly $\ker D_K$. Indeed, express an arbitrary tensor as $z=\sum_{i=1}^r b_i\otimes w_i$ with the $b_i\in K$ linearly independent over $k$, by collecting its finitely many coefficients in a basis of their span. If $D_K(z)=0$, apply a $k$-linear functional on $K$ taking $b_i$ to $1$ and the other $b_j$ to $0$ (extend the finite independent family to a basis). This gives $D(w_i)=0$, hence $w_i\in W^G$ by step 2. Conversely $D_K$ kills each $b\otimes w$ with $w\in W^G$, and hence their sums. This proves the image equality directly, without assuming a tensor-exactness theorem or commuting an infinite intersection with tensor product.

source.place: Proposition 4.31, p.96, coefficient-basis argument; Corollary 4.34, p.97

proof.text: Put $A_K=K\otimes_k A$. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], $G_K=G\times_k\operatorname{Spec}K$ is $\operatorname{Spec}A_K$. Since $G\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth, [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced] says its fibre over the unique point of $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is geometrically reduced. That fibre is $G$ itself, so $G_K$ is reduced. The equivalence in [def-pc-reduced-scheme] then makes $A_K$ a reduced ring. If $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ generate $A$ over $k$, the elements $1\otimes a_j$ generate $A_K$ over $K$, by expanding polynomials and pure tensors. Thus $A_K$ is a reduced finitely generated $K$-algebra, precisely the hypotheses needed for the vanishing principle in the next step.

source.place: Propositions 1.10, 1.26(b), pp.9--13; Stacks Tag 056T, lemma-smooth-geometrically-normal; Tag 01I4, lemma-fibre-product-affine-schemes

proof.text: Let $z\in K\otimes_k W$ be fixed by every $g\in G(K)$. Choose a $k$-basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ of $W$ and write $D_K(z)=\sum_{j=1}^d f_j\otimes e_j$ with $f_j\in A_K$. Every $K$-algebra homomorphism $\phi:A_K\to K$ has the form $b\otimes a\mapsto b\,g(a)$ for a unique $k$-algebra homomorphism $g:A\to K$, by [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property]. Step 2 gives $\sum_j\phi(f_j)e_j=gz-z=0$. Linear independence of the $e_j$ over $K$ implies $\phi(f_j)=0$ for every $\phi$. Apply clause (2) of [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing] to $A_K$ over the algebraically closed field $K$, using step 4: each $f_j=0$. Hence $D_K(z)=0$. Conversely, step 2 shows that $D_K(z)=0$ implies $gz=z$ for every $g\in G(K)$. The geometric fixed vectors are therefore $\ker D_K$, which is the image computed in step 3.

source.place: Propositions 4.32--4.33, p.96, with coefficient-function detection from Proposition 1.10, pp.9--10

proof.text: Finally, the inclusion $W^G\hookrightarrow W$ has a $k$-linear retraction: extend a basis of $W^G$ to one of $W$ and kill the added basis vectors. Tensoring the inclusion and this retraction with $K$ gives maps whose composite is the identity (check on pure tensors); the scalar-extended inclusion is therefore injective. If $0\ne w\in W^G$, a $k$-linear functional $\lambda:W\to k$ with $\lambda(w)=1$ gives $(1_K\otimes\lambda)(1\otimes w)=1$, so its image is a nonzero geometric fixed vector. Conversely $W^G=0$ makes its tensor product and thus the fixed subspace zero by steps 3 and 5. The same proof allows $d=0$, the trivial group, and disconnected smooth groups. Smoothness was used only in step 4; no perfectness of $k$ or connectedness of $G$ was used.

source.place: Corollary 4.34, p.97, and its application in Corollary 14.12, p.283; elementary basis argument for injectivity and nonzero detection
